passage: Chetan, your face tells me the office is asking for Sundays again. Sit. Your Irawati-aaji was twenty when the manager at the export house in Bhiwandi told us girls to come in every Sunday, with no extra pay. 'Your growth will suffer if you don't,' he said, 'and this stays inside these walls.' I was frightened, and I also felt I owed them, because they had hired a girl with only a school certificate. So I went, four Sundays. But I wrote each date in the back of my ration notebook, with the hours. Then I showed the notebook to Kamala-tai, who knew the rules because her husband was in the workers' union. She read my appointment letter with me, line by line, and took me to the union office. I didn't storm out. I went back on Monday with the notebook and someone beside me. The Sundays stopped. Keep your own notebook, Chetan.

qa.q: Where did Irawati write the dates and hours?
qa.a: Irawati wrote them in the back of her ration notebook.

qa.q: How did young Irawati feel about the unpaid Sundays?
qa.a: Irawati felt frightened and also indebted to the company, which kept her going for four Sundays.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed things for Irawati?
qa.a: Showing the notebook to Kamala-tai, reading the appointment letter together, and going to the union office before facing the manager.

qa.q: How might Kamala-tai have seen young Irawati's notebook?
qa.a: Kamala-tai likely saw it as clear evidence and a reason to help, which is why she read the letter with Irawati and took her to the union office.

grounding: A grandmother recalls unpaid Sundays demanded under threat and secrecy, and how written records, reading her appointment letter and support from the union helped before quitting in anger.

passage: Her team lead's message came on Friday at 7 p.m., just as Pallavi was packing for the overnight bus home for Ganesh Chaturthi: 'Need you Sat and Sun. No OT, but your growth depends on commitment. Don't discuss with the team.' It was the third weekend in six. The one senior she trusted was on leave, and her bus left at ten. Her fingers hovered over a resignation email. Instead she called her college friend Ishita, who worked in HR at another company. 'Don't quit tonight,' Ishita said. 'Screenshot that message. Find your offer letter and see what it says about working hours. On Monday we'll work out who you can talk to, your HR or the labour department's helpline.' Pallavi saved everything into a folder named 'weekends', replied, 'I'm travelling for the festival, will discuss Monday,' and caught her bus with four minutes to spare.

qa.q: At what time did the team lead's message come?
qa.a: The message came on Friday at 7 p.m.

qa.q: What was Pallavi feeling as her fingers hovered over the resignation email?
qa.a: Pallavi felt angry and cornered, and afraid of being pushed into another unpaid weekend.

qa.q: Why was Ishita's advice better than quitting that night?
qa.a: Keeping screenshots, checking the offer letter and finding the right person to talk to builds a record and support, while quitting in anger would lose both.

qa.q: How does the team lead seem to see weekend work?
qa.a: The team lead treats it as a test of commitment and wants it kept quiet, which suggests they know it may not be fair.

grounding: Shows unpaid weekend work demanded with a threat and a request for silence, and Pallavi keeping records, checking her terms and seeking support instead of resigning in anger.

passage: Trisha, when your phone buzzes and you jump like that, it reminds me of myself at twenty-two. Your Suraj-mama had a supervisor at a medicine warehouse in Baddi who shouted on every call. After a month, just the ringtone made my stomach drop. I froze. For three years I stayed, telling myself any other place would be worse. Then one night my friend Pinto made me write two lists: what could really happen if I left, and what I only imagined. Real: a few lean months. Imagined: that nobody would ever hire me again. After that I did boring things. I put a little aside each month. I called four old classmates and asked about openings. When the next shouting call came, my stomach still dropped, but now I knew it was telling me something. Eight months later I left. So listen to that stomach, Trisha. Then make your lists.

qa.q: Where was the warehouse?
qa.a: The warehouse was in Baddi.

qa.q: How did young Suraj feel when the ringtone went off?
qa.a: Suraj felt dread and fear, with a dropping stomach at the sound.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Suraj stop freezing?
qa.a: Pinto's two lists, separating real risks from imagined ones, which led him to build a cushion and contacts before leaving.

qa.q: Why might Pinto have suggested the two lists?
qa.a: Pinto likely saw that Suraj's fear was mixing real and imagined dangers, and wanted Suraj to see which ones could actually be planned for.

grounding: An uncle recalls years frozen by dread of a shouting supervisor, and learning to treat the fear as information, sort real from imagined risk and build a safety net.

passage: Deepak was at his cousin's wedding in Jaipur, dhol thumping, when his phone buzzed for the ninth time that day. 'Call me. Now.' His manager, Mr. Batra, again. Deepak's stomach dropped the way it always did, and he slipped behind the tent, where it was only slightly quieter. His friend Simran followed him out. 'You've gone grey. What's he going to do, fire you at a wedding?' Deepak laughed weakly, then didn't. 'He could block my confirmation.' 'Could he, really? Or is that the fear talking?' Between the generator and the catering vans they sorted it out: real risk, a bad review next month; imagined risk, being ruined forever. Simran made him name three college friends who could tell him about openings, and suggested he talk to his elder brother about a backup for a few lean months. Deepak texted Mr. Batra: 'At a family wedding today, will call at 9 a.m. tomorrow.' Then he went back in and danced, badly.

qa.q: How many times had Deepak's phone buzzed that day?
qa.a: Deepak's phone had buzzed nine times that day.

qa.q: What does Deepak's stomach dropping suggest about his feelings?
qa.a: It suggests Deepak feels dread and fear whenever Mr. Batra messages, even at a family wedding.

qa.q: Why was sorting real risks from imagined ones useful?
qa.a: It showed the likely worst case was a bad review, not ruin, and led to a plan with college contacts and a backup for lean months.

qa.q: How does Simran see Deepak's fear?
qa.a: Simran sees it as partly real and partly the fear talking, and helps pull the two apart.

grounding: Shows a young employee whose body reacts to every message from his manager, and a friend helping him separate real from imagined risk and plan a safety net.

passage: In the kitchen of the beach hotel in Goa, Chef Fernandes threw a tray of undercooked prawns into the sink and said, loud enough for the whole line, 'This is why nobody wanted to hire a village boy.' Yusuf kept his head down. Later, peeling onions, he told Minakshi from pastry, 'He's the one who took me when no one else would. I owe him.' Minakshi wiped her hands. 'You owe him thanks. You don't owe him your dignity.' Yusuf thought about it through the whole dinner service. The next morning, before prep, he knocked on the chef's office door. 'Chef, I'm grateful you gave me this job. I'll always remember that. But please don't speak to me like that in front of the line again. If the prawns are wrong, tell me what to fix.' Chef Fernandes stared, then grunted, 'Get back to work.' That day he didn't shout at Yusuf.

qa.q: What did Chef Fernandes throw into the sink?
qa.a: Chef Fernandes threw a tray of undercooked prawns into the sink.

qa.q: What did Yusuf feel toward Chef Fernandes while peeling onions?
qa.a: Yusuf felt grateful and indebted, which made him excuse the humiliation.

qa.q: What did Yusuf's words to the chef get right?
qa.a: He thanked the chef for the past while clearly refusing the present treatment and asking for direct feedback instead.

qa.q: How does Minakshi see Yusuf's sense of debt?
qa.a: Minakshi sees that thanks is owed but dignity is not, and pushes Yusuf to separate the two.

grounding: Shows gratitude to a boss who gave Yusuf his start keeping him silent about abuse, until he thanks him for the past and refuses the present treatment.

passage:
Dear Uday-sir,
I've started this email four times. You gave me my first break at the studio when my portfolio was three drawings and a lot of hope, and you convinced the partners to take a chance on me. I haven't forgotten that, and I never will.
But in the last two months you have called me 'useless' in front of clients twice, and last Friday you threw my sketchbook on the floor. I kept telling myself that someone who helped me so much must have the right. I don't think that's true anymore.
I'm still grateful. I also need this to stop. From now on, if my work is wrong, please tell me what to change, privately. If that can't happen, I'll need to speak to the partners.
I'd like to keep working with you.
With respect,
Vikas

qa.q: How many times had Uday-sir called Vikas 'useless' in front of clients?
qa.a: Uday-sir had done it twice in the last two months.

qa.q: What mix of feelings shows in Vikas's email?
qa.a: Vikas feels grateful for the first break and hurt by the recent treatment, torn between loyalty and self-respect.

qa.q: What makes Vikas's email a wise approach?
qa.a: It thanks Uday-sir for the past, names the specific behaviour, asks for private feedback, and says what Vikas will do if it continues.

qa.q: How might Uday-sir react to reading this email?
qa.a: Uday-sir may feel surprised or stung to be named, but also reminded that Vikas values the relationship and wants to keep working together.

grounding: An email shows Vikas thanking a boss for a first break while refusing to keep excusing the boss's humiliating treatment.

passage: At 11 p.m. in her Hyderabad flat, Rekha finished the email. Subject line: 'The truth about how Akash treats his team.' Three paragraphs, every insult he had thrown at her in the last month, addressed to all 340 people in the company. Her heart was pounding and it felt wonderful. Her finger was on send when her roommate came in with two cups of ginger tea and read over her shoulder. 'It's all true,' the roommate said. 'And it'll make you the story instead of him.' Rekha moved the draft to a folder and went to bed angry. In the morning the anger was still there, but quieter. She opened a new email, addressed only to HR, and wrote two paragraphs: three dates, exact quotes, the names of two colleagues who had been present. No adjectives. She read it twice, attached her notes and sent it at 10 a.m.

qa.q: How many people was the first email addressed to?
qa.a: It was addressed to all 340 people in the company.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling as her finger hovered on send?
qa.a: Rekha felt furious and a rush of satisfaction, her heart pounding.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Keeping the angry draft unsent and writing a calm, factual complaint to HR, because it raised the problem without costing her reputation or reference.

qa.q: How does Rekha's roommate see the angry email?
qa.a: The roommate sees it as true but risky, likely to make Rekha the story instead of Akash.

grounding: Shows valid fury at a manager poured into an unsent all-company email, then cooled into one calm, documented complaint to HR.

passage:
'Listen to this before I post it in the company group.' Sunaina pressed play. Her own voice filled the café, shaking: '...and Mr. Shetty thinks it's funny to throw files at interns...'
'Stop it there,' Yamini said. 'Is it true?'
'Every word. He threw my file today.'
'Then it matters too much to waste on a voice note.'
'I want everyone to know.'
'I know you do. You're allowed to be this angry. But if you post it, what happens tomorrow?'
Sunaina stared at her cold coffee. 'He says I'm unstable. HR deletes it. And I lose the reference for my master's application.'
'So keep it. Don't delete it, don't send it. Tomorrow, when you're calmer, write down today's date, what he did, who saw it. Send that to HR. One page.'
'That feels so small.'
'It's small and on record. The voice note is loud and gone in a day.'
Sunaina saved the voice note in a private folder.

qa.a: Mr. Shetty threw Sunaina's file.

qa.q: How can you tell Sunaina is very angry?

qa.q: What would you advise Sunaina to do tomorrow?

qa.q: What would change if Sunaina posted the voice note?
qa.a: Mr. Shetty could call her unstable, HR might delete it, and she could lose the reference she needs for her master's.

passage: At the dairy cooperative's collection centre outside Anand, the supervisor, Mr. Parmar, had a habit of shouting at whoever handled the evening milk register. For weeks Devika thought it was about her slow handwriting. Then one evening, waiting for the last tanker, Sahil from the testing counter said quietly, 'He yelled at me for forty minutes last month. I stopped sleeping properly.' Devika felt her shoulders loosen for the first time in weeks. It wasn't just her. They sat on the steps and compared dates, not rumours: she had four, he had three. 'Don't ask the others to join in,' Sahil said. 'Ramila-ben has a small baby, she can't risk anything.' Devika nodded. 'Just facts. And we each keep our own notes.' They agreed that if it went on, each of them would speak to the society's secretary with what they had written. Then the tanker's lights came up the road.

qa.q: How many dates did Devika have?
qa.a: Devika had four dates.

qa.q: What was Devika feeling when Sahil admitted the same treatment?
qa.a: Devika felt relieved, her shoulders loosening, knowing it wasn't just her.

qa.q: What made their way of comparing notes wise?
qa.a: They shared dates rather than rumours, kept Ramila-ben out of any risk, and planned to each speak to the society's secretary.

qa.q: What has the shouting been like for Sahil?
qa.a: Sahil has been badly shaken, even losing sleep after being yelled at for forty minutes.

grounding: Shows a coworker admitting he faces the same shouting, the relief of not being alone, and comparing facts without drawing others into a risky move.

passage: Amandeep's month had been a seesaw. On Monday Farhan, who owned the small printing shop in Ludhiana, called him 'my best boy' and bought him lassi. On Wednesday he screamed about a misprint and said, 'Nobody else would hire you. Remember that.' By Friday Amandeep felt dizzy just walking in, as if the floor tilted with Farhan's moods. He had only enough in his pocket for bus fare that week, so quitting felt impossible. On Sunday his old school teacher, Gill-sir, met him at the gurdwara langar and noticed. 'You look like someone holding his breath.' Amandeep told him everything. Gill-sir didn't tell him to quit. 'Test what he says. Apply to two shops. See if it's true.' On Monday Amandeep sent his CV to two printing presses on the same street. One called back that evening for an interview.

qa.q: What did Farhan call Amandeep on Monday?
qa.a: Farhan called him 'my best boy'.

qa.q: What was Amandeep feeling by Friday?
qa.a: Amandeep felt dizzy and anxious, as if the floor tilted with Farhan's moods.

qa.q: Why was Gill-sir's advice wise?
qa.a: Applying to two shops tested Farhan's claim that nobody else would hire him, and the quick callback showed it was false.

qa.q: How does Gill-sir read Amandeep at the langar?
qa.a: Gill-sir sees someone holding his breath, tense and trapped, and cares enough to ask.

grounding: Shows a boss swinging between praise and threats to make Amandeep feel dependent, and testing that claim by applying elsewhere with an outside mentor's help.

passage: Mr. Menon ran the event-management firm in Kochi like the weather. One week he told clients Yash was 'the future of this company'; the next he called Yash into the cabin and said, 'Leave, and I'll make sure no agency in this city touches you. Nobody else would hire you anyway.' Yash, eight months into the job, began to believe it. He stopped telling his elder sister Uma about work because every story sounded like complaining. One Sunday she found him at 1 a.m. still answering Mr. Menon's messages. 'Show me,' she said. He did. She scrolled through a week of it: praise, threat, praise, threat. 'This is a pattern, Yash. And the "nobody would hire you" part is something you can check.' Together they updated his CV that night. By Wednesday he had applied to three agencies, and he had told two college friends what was really going on.

qa.q: How long had Yash been in the job?
qa.a: Yash had been in the job eight months.

qa.q: What was Yash feeling when he stopped telling Uma about work?
qa.a: Yash felt ashamed and worn down, afraid every story would sound like complaining.

qa.q: What steps helped Yash see through Mr. Menon's claim?
qa.a: Uma helping him see the praise-threat pattern, updating his CV, applying to three agencies, and telling two friends.

qa.q: What is it like for Uma to find Yash answering messages at 1 a.m.?
qa.a: Uma is worried, and wants to see the messages so she can help him name the pattern.

grounding: Shows a boss alternating praise and threats and claiming nobody else would hire Yash, and his sister helping him spot the pattern and test the claim.

passage: Kavitha's pay from the garment unit in Tiruppur covered her younger brother's college fees and most of the rent since Appa's accident. So when the floor supervisor, Harish, called her 'slow cow' in front of the line, she swallowed it. The other women said, 'That's just how supervisors are.' For a while she repeated it to herself too. Then one night, eating cold rice after a twelve-hour shift, she caught herself thinking she deserved it. That frightened her more than Harish did. She couldn't quit; that was simply true. But she could stop calling it normal. She started eating lunch outside, away from the line, even for ten minutes. She wrote Harish's words in a small notebook with dates. On Sundays she went to the tailoring class at the church hall, three hours of learning a skill that might one day be her own shop.

qa.q: Where did Kavitha go on Sundays?
qa.a: Kavitha went to the tailoring class at the church hall.

qa.q: What did Kavitha feel when she caught herself thinking she deserved it?
qa.a: Kavitha felt frightened, because it meant she was starting to accept the abuse as normal.

qa.q: What small ways did Kavitha protect her dignity while staying?
qa.a: Eating lunch outside away from the line, noting Harish's words with dates, and learning tailoring on Sundays as a way out.

qa.q: How do the other women on the line see Harish's behaviour?
qa.a: They see it as just how supervisors are, which makes it harder for Kavitha to name it as wrong.

grounding: Shows a worker who must keep the job for her family, refusing to call the abuse normal and protecting her dignity while building a way out.

passage:
'You're home late again, akka.'
'Mrs. Varma kept me back to redo the accounts. Then she said I should be grateful she doesn't cut my pay.'
Harish put down his textbook. 'Should you quit?'
'I can't, Harish. Your fees. Amma's medicines. This job is the only fixed money we have.'
'Then just adjust. Everyone's boss is like that.'
'No.' Chandrika's voice was sharper than she meant. 'That's the part I won't do. I'll stay because I have to. But I'm not going to pretend it's normal.'
'So what then?'
'I've applied for the bank clerk exam in March. I'm studying on the bus. And I leave at seven now, whatever she says, unless it's truly urgent.'
'She'll be angry.'
'Maybe. I'll handle it.'
Harish was quiet, then pushed his textbook aside. 'Want me to quiz you on the reasoning section?'
Chandrika laughed for the first time that day. 'Yes.'

qa.q: When is the bank clerk exam Chandrika applied for?
qa.a: The exam is in March.

qa.q: What does Chandrika's sharp 'No' suggest she is feeling?
qa.a: It suggests she feels frustrated and determined, refusing to accept the treatment as normal even though she has to stay.

qa.q: Why is Chandrika's plan a wise one?
qa.a: She stays for the income while studying for the March exam and leaving at seven, which protects her health and builds a way out.

qa.q: How does Harish first see Chandrika's situation, and how does that change?
qa.a: Harish first thinks she should just adjust, then understands and offers to quiz her.

grounding: Shows the real constraint of needing a salary for the family, and Chandrika staying while refusing to call the treatment normal and planning her exit.

passage: Monday, 11 p.m. Divyansh's diary. Week seven of the 'internship' at the marketing agency. Today I made 42 cold calls, formatted Kashish-ma'am's slides and fetched lunch for the whole team. I've learned nothing new since week two. No stipend, and every time I ask about the 'full-time role after', the answer is 'let's see'. I feel used, and I also feel scared, because this is the only line on my CV that isn't college. So here's the plan, written down so I can't back out. Tomorrow I ask Kashish-ma'am for fifteen minutes. Three questions: is there any stipend, what exactly will I learn in the next month, and when will the full-time decision be made. I'll give it until the end of next month. If nothing changes by then, I leave and keep the seven weeks on my CV anyway. That line is already mine.

qa.q: How many cold calls did Divyansh make today?
qa.a: Divyansh made 42 cold calls today.

qa.q: What two feelings pull at Divyansh?
qa.a: Divyansh feels used, and also scared of losing the only non-college line on the CV.

qa.q: Why is Divyansh's plan a good one?
qa.a: Asking about a stipend, learning and a decision date, then setting a deadline to leave, stops the unpaid work from running on forever.

qa.q: How might Kashish-ma'am see Divyansh's request for fifteen minutes?
qa.a: Kashish-ma'am may be surprised, but it gives a clear chance to explain what the internship offers or to admit it offers little.

grounding: A diary shows an unpaid internship that is really full-time work, and a plan to ask about stipend and learning goals, set a time limit and walk if nothing changes.

passage: 'We took you without any experience, Nirmala. That's a big favour,' the owner had said on her first day at the small architecture firm in Ahmedabad. When her classmate Himani asked why she'd skipped their college reunion, Nirmala said, 'I owe them.' Himani frowned. 'Owe them what? You're drafting their plans for a small stipend. The next day, when the owner asked her to pick up his dry cleaning, she said politely, 'I'd rather spend that hour on the site drawings, sir. I'm here to learn.' He looked surprised. passage:
'They said it again,' Naveen muttered, dropping into a chair in the break room. 'I asked for Sunday off for my cousin's engagement, and they said, "We're doing you a favour by having you here."'
Pooja, a year ahead of him in the same programme, put down her sandwich. 'And you said?'

passage: Gurleen, you keep talking about your manager at the lab. Good. Let your Raghav-mama tell you about Mrs. Sethi. I was twenty, an intern at a small newspaper in Amritsar, and every other editor made me fetch tea. Mrs. Sethi gave me real stories, a water shortage, a school fire, and sat with my drafts, red pen and all, never raising her voice. I admired her so much I tried to become her. I stayed till midnight to impress her, skipped my own exam revision, stopped seeing friends. One day she noticed and said, 'Raghav, I want you good, not exhausted.' That stung, and it taught me. Before I left, I asked her for a reference letter, and I took every note on it seriously. I wrote to her every Diwali for thirty years. She came to my wedding. So admire her, Gurleen. Learn everything. But sleep, and see your friends.

qa.a: The small newspaper was in Amritsar.

qa.q: How did young Raghav feel about Mrs. Sethi?
qa.a: Raghav felt deep admiration for her, enough to try to become her.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Raghav learn from Mrs. Sethi in a healthy way?
qa.a: Her telling him she wanted him good, not exhausted, after which he kept learning but looked after himself, asked for a reference and kept in touch.

qa.q: How might Mrs. Sethi have felt seeing Raghav stay till midnight?
qa.a: Mrs. Sethi was probably concerned rather than impressed, which is why she said she wanted him good, not exhausted.

grounding: An uncle recalls admiring a patient manager who taught him properly, overdoing it at the cost of his own needs, and then asking for a reference and keeping the bond for life.

passage: Trisha had one week left with Zainab, the only manager at the health NGO in Pune who had ever taught her properly. Zainab had shown her how to clean survey data, let her present to the director, and answered every silly question with the same calm patience of hers. Now Zainab was transferring to the Lucknow office on Friday, and the whole team was in chaos over a funder's deadline. Trisha had spent days wanting to say something big and grateful, and saying nothing. On Thursday, in the only free ten minutes, she asked: 'Could you write me a reference? And would you tell me honestly what I should work on?' Zainab smiled. 'Yes to both. Your analysis is strong. Your emails are too long.' Trisha laughed and wrote it down. That evening she went to her cousin's birthday dinner instead of staying late, something she had skipped twice for work. On Friday she saved Zainab's personal email.

qa.q: Where was Zainab transferring to?
qa.a: Zainab was transferring to the Lucknow office.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling during the days she said nothing?
qa.a: Trisha felt grateful and a little shy, wanting to say something big but holding back.

qa.q: What did Trisha ask for, and why was it wise?
qa.a: A reference and honest feedback, which turned admiration into something useful she can carry forward.

qa.q: How does Zainab respond to Trisha's request?
qa.a: Zainab is pleased to help, giving a yes to both and honest feedback about long emails.

grounding: Shows admiration for a manager who teaches patiently, turned under time pressure into a reference request, feedback and a lasting contact, without neglecting other needs.
